title: Natural selection
summary: How variation, overproduction and selection pressures drive evolution, how sexual selection works, and how allele frequencies in gene pools change.

keyterms.definition: Process by which individuals with heritable traits better suited to the environment survive and reproduce more, passing those traits on.
Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations.
Random change in the base sequence of DNA; the original source of new alleles and so of variation.
Populations produce more offspring than the environment can support, leading to competition for limited resources.
A biotic or abiotic factor that affects the survival or reproduction of individuals differently according to their traits.
A heritable characteristic that makes an individual suited to its environment and way of life.
A trait developed during an individual's life (e.g. by use or training); not inherited, so cannot drive evolution.
Selection arising from differences in mating success, e.g. female choice of males with elaborate displays.
All the genes and their different alleles present in an interbreeding population.
The proportion of all copies of a gene in a gene pool that are a particular allele, from 0 to 1.
Selection favouring individuals at one extreme of a range of variation, shifting the mean.
Selection against both extremes, favouring intermediate phenotypes and reducing variation.
Selection favouring both extremes over intermediates, which may split a population into two forms.
p² + 2pq + q² = 1, relating allele frequencies (p, q) to genotype frequencies in a population in genetic equilibrium.
Humans deliberately choosing individuals with desired traits to breed, changing domesticated species over generations.

questions.prompt: What is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?
options: Meiosis
Fertilization
Natural selection
Mutation
questions.explanation: Only mutation creates new alleles. Meiosis and fertilization (sexual reproduction) reshuffle existing alleles into new combinations; selection acts on the variation produced.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of natural selection.
items: Variation exists between individuals in a population
More offspring are produced than the environment can support
Individuals better adapted to the environment survive and reproduce more
They pass on their heritable traits, so these become more frequent
questions.explanation: Variation plus overproduction leads to a struggle for survival; differential survival and reproduction of heritable traits changes the population over generations.

questions.statement: A giraffe that stretches its neck during its life will pass a longer neck on to its offspring.
questions.explanation: Acquired characteristics do not change the genes in gametes, so they are not inherited. Only heritable variation can be acted on by natural selection.

questions.text: Because populations produce more offspring than resources can support, individuals experience ___ for resources.
questions.explanation: Overproduction means not all offspring can survive. Those with traits that help them obtain limited resources are more likely to survive.

questions.prompt: Which is an abiotic selection pressure?
options: Low soil water availability
Predation
Disease
Competition with another species
questions.explanation: Abiotic factors are non-living, e.g. temperature, water availability, salinity, soil pH. Predation, disease and competition are biotic factors.

questions.prompt: Match each source of variation to how it generates variation.

pairs.right: New allele combinations on a chromosome
Random mixes of maternal and paternal chromosomes

questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction (meiosis and fertilization) reshuffles alleles; mutation is the only process that produces genuinely new alleles.

questions.statement: Natural selection acts on individuals, but it is populations that evolve.
questions.explanation: An individual's genes do not change through selection. Differential survival and reproduction change allele frequencies in the population over generations.

questions.text: All the genes and alleles in an interbreeding population make up its ___.
questions.explanation: A genome is the genetic material of one organism; the gene pool includes all alleles of the whole population.

questions.prompt: Why must a trait be heritable for natural selection to cause evolution?
options: Only heritable traits are affected by the environment
Non-heritable traits always reduce survival
Only heritable traits can be passed to offspring, changing the next generation
Heritable traits mutate more often
questions.explanation: If a trait that improves survival is not inherited, the offspring do not benefit from it and the population does not change.

questions.prompt: Which statement about adaptation is correct?
options: Individuals develop adaptations because they need them
Adaptations are heritable traits that became common because they increased survival and reproduction
Adaptations appear in response to selection pressures in one generation
An adaptation is any change during an organism's life
questions.explanation: Variation arises randomly (mutation, sexual reproduction), not in response to need. Selection then makes beneficial variants more common over many generations.

questions.prompt: Male birds of paradise have elaborate plumage and courtship displays. What best explains this?
options: Bright plumage camouflages them from predators
Females choose to mate with males with the most impressive displays
Displays are learned and passed on culturally
Bright plumage helps regulate body temperature
questions.explanation: This is sexual selection: male traits that increase mating success spread, even if they increase predation risk, because they indicate fitness to choosy females.

questions.statement: Sexual selection can favour traits that reduce an individual's chance of survival.
questions.explanation: A conspicuous trait may attract predators, but if it increases mating success enough, its alleles are still passed on more often.

questions.prompt: In Endler's studies, how did male guppy colouration differ between streams?
options: Males were more brightly coloured where predation was intense
Males were equally colourful in all streams
Females were more colourful than males where predators were absent
Males were more brightly coloured where predation was low
questions.explanation: Strong predation selects against conspicuous males (natural selection), while female preference selects for bright colours (sexual selection). Where predation is weak, sexual selection dominates.

questions.text: In Endler's guppies, predators favour drab males through natural selection, while females favour colourful males through ___ selection.
questions.explanation: The balance between these two opposing pressures determines how colourful males are in each population.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of Endler's field experiment.
items: Observe that colour differs between high- and low-predation streams
Hypothesize that predation pressure determines colour
Transfer guppies from a high-predation site to a low-predation stream
Monitor male colouration over many generations
Males in the new site became more colourful
questions.explanation: Moving populations tested the hypothesis: removing strong predation allowed sexual selection to increase male colour within a few years (many guppy generations).

questions.prompt: Match each selection type to its example.

pairs.right: Females prefer brightly coloured male guppies
Drought kills plants with shallow roots

questions.explanation: Sexual selection depends on mating success; natural selection depends on survival in the face of living or non-living factors.

questions.statement: In Endler's laboratory experiments, guppies were also found to match the size of gravel in their pools when predators were present.
questions.explanation: With predators, males evolved spots that blended with the background gravel (camouflage). Without predators, spots became larger and more conspicuous.

questions.prompt: Why are Endler's experiments useful models of selection?
options: Guppies have a short generation time, so evolution can be observed over a few years
Guppies cannot mutate
Guppies only reproduce asexually
Guppies have no predators in the wild
questions.explanation: Short generations mean many generations occur within an experiment, so changes in heritable traits can be measured and linked to controlled selection pressures.

questions.text: Evolution is defined as a change in the ___ characteristics of a population over generations.
questions.explanation: Only inherited traits link one generation to the next, so only changes in them count as evolution.

questions.prompt: Which observation would suggest a trait in guppies is NOT heritable?
options: Offspring of bright males are bright when raised in the same conditions
Offspring of bright and drab males reared in identical conditions show the same colour
Colour changes over generations after predators are removed
Colour varies between populations
questions.explanation: If parental colour does not predict offspring colour under identical conditions, variation is environmental and selection on it could not cause evolution.

questions.prompt: In a population, 16% of individuals show a recessive phenotype (aa). What is the frequency of allele A?

questions.text: If q = 0.2, the expected frequency of heterozygotes (2pq) is ___.

questions.statement: A population in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium must have random mating, no mutation, no gene flow, no selection and a large population size.
questions.explanation: If any condition is violated, allele frequencies can change. Real populations rarely meet all conditions, so deviation from expected frequencies indicates evolution.

questions.prompt: Match each pattern of selection to its example.

pairs.right: Human birth weight near the average favoured
Small and large beaks favoured, medium selected against

questions.explanation: Stabilizing favours the mean, directional favours one extreme, disruptive favours both extremes.

questions.prompt: Which change in a frequency distribution indicates disruptive selection?
options: The mean shifts to one side
The curve becomes narrower around the mean
The distribution does not change
The curve becomes bimodal with fewer intermediates
questions.explanation: Intermediates are selected against, so two peaks develop at the extremes. Narrowing indicates stabilizing selection; a shift in mean indicates directional selection.

questions.prompt: Why do allele frequencies often differ between geographically isolated populations of the same species?
options: Isolated populations do not undergo mutation
There is no gene flow between them, and they experience different selection pressures and chance effects
Isolation always causes all alleles to be lost
Allele frequencies are fixed for a species
questions.explanation: Without interbreeding, changes in one gene pool are not shared. Different environments select different alleles, and random changes accumulate separately. Online databases show such differences, e.g. in ABO frequencies.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for calculating the carrier frequency of a recessive condition.
items: Find the frequency of affected individuals (q²)
Take the square root to find q
questions.explanation: Only the homozygous recessive phenotype can be identified directly, so start from q² and work out p before using 2pq.

questions.text: Cabbage, broccoli, cauliflower and kale were all produced from wild mustard (Brassica oleracea) by ___ selection.
questions.explanation: Breeders repeatedly chose plants with enlarged leaves, buds or flower heads to breed, producing very different crops from one species.

questions.statement: In artificial selection, the selection pressure is the deliberate choice of breeding individuals by humans rather than the environment.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is the same as natural selection (heritable variation, differential reproduction), but humans decide which individuals reproduce.

questions.prompt: How does natural selection change a gene pool?
options: Individuals with advantageous heritable traits reproduce more, so their alleles increase in frequency
It creates new alleles that the environment requires
It changes the alleles in individuals' body cells
It keeps allele frequencies constant
questions.explanation: Selection does not create alleles; it changes their frequencies through differential reproductive success.
